pass_a_gloss: What is the reason for the silence of the many, and especially now, and for me, who am being forced to be silent, both willingly and unwillingly, and to be silent under compulsion? For I have neglected, in a certain way, the good and beautiful words, which are spoken or written by the chosen and approved men, with a certain unimpeded flow of words and names, in order. But I, who am less capable of this charming task, a genuinely Greek work, have not been able to accomplish it. But now, for eight years, I have not been able, either myself to say or write anything, great or small, nor have I heard from another, who writes or speaks privately, or who delivers panegyric and forensic speeches, except from those wonderful men, who have practiced the beautiful philosophy, for whom elegance of language and refinement of names are of less concern. And when they place their voices in a secondary position, they wish to examine and proclaim the matters themselves, with precision, not because they do not want to, but because they want very much to express the good and precise thoughts, but perhaps they are not able, since they have the sacred and divine word in their minds, and the word that is in their words is elegant, to encompass two possessions of each human being, with one and the same, and small and human soul, which are very contrary. For if silence is a friend and helper, and silence is a helper, in speech, you will not find it anywhere else, but in voices and the continuous practice of them. But now, I want to say something, even if it is small, to the voice of the Greeks, our wonderful teachers, who now direct the affairs of all human beings under the Roman authority, which is powerful and boastful, and imitative, but burdensome to me. But since our words are certain images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters, and with skill, and with the material of colors, not only similar, but also varied and beautiful, with many-blended mixture of flowers, to write and paint, without being hindered, we would agree.
pass_b_english: What is the reason for the silence of the many others, many times over, and especially now for me, who am being forced to keep silent both willingly and unwillingly, and being compelled to hold my tongue? For I have neglected, in a certain way, the good and beautiful words, which are spoken or composed by the chosen and approved men, with their distinguished names and words, in a certain unimpeded sequence. But I, being less naturally gifted for this charming task — a genuinely Greek work — have not been able to accomplish it. Yet now eight years have already passed for me, during which I have not been able either myself to say or write anything at all, great or small, nor have I heard from another who writes or speaks privately, or who delivers panegyric and forensic speeches publicly, except from those wonderful men who have cultivated the beautiful philosophy. For them, elegance of language and refinement of names are of less concern; they place their voices in a secondary position, wishing to examine and proclaim the matters themselves, with precision. They do this not because they do not want to, but because they want very much to express the good and precise thoughts with ease and elegance in speech. But perhaps they are not able, since they would need to encompass two possessions of each human being — the sacred and divinely given mind, and the word that is elegant in its words — with one and the same small and human soul, things that are utterly opposed to each other. For if silence is a friend and helper in some way, and silence is a helper, you will not find the well‑spoken word anywhere else except in voices and their continuous practice. But now the mind seizes on some other lesson terribly, and binds the mouth — the tongue — if I should wish to utter even something small in the Greek voice. Our wonderful teachers now direct the affairs of all human beings under the Roman authority, not confused nor learning wretchedly, but being themselves eloquent, precise, varied, and wonderful, and, to sum it up, most Greek in expression. Yet they have been handed over to the Roman voice — imposing, boastful, and conforming itself to the royal authority — but burdensome to me. Still, it could not have been otherwise, nor would it have been possible for me to wish it otherwise at any time. Since our words are certain images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak — like good painters, most skilled in technique, and rich in the material of colors — we would agree that they can paint not only likenesses, but also varied and surpassingly beautiful pictures, with the many‑blended mixture of flowers, without being hindered in any way.
notes: The text is a panegyric to Origen, and the author is discussing the importance of silence and speech in relation to the pursuit of wisdom and philosophy.

review.notes: Pass A is incomplete compared to the Locked Greek. It omits the entire clause: 'καὶ τὸ στόμα συνδεῖ τὴν γλῶτταν' (and the mouth binds the tongue) and the description of the teachers: 'οἱ ϑαιμαστοὶ ἡμῶν... οὔτε καὶ ἐκμανϑανόμενοι ἀταλαιττώρως ὄντες μὲν αὑτοὶ 00(p)oi τε καὶ ἀκρλιβεῖς καὶ ποιχίλοι χαὶ ϑαυμαστοὶ, καὶ συνελόντα εἰττεῖν Ελληνιχώτατοι' (our wonderful teachers... not being confused nor learning wretchedly, but being themselves eloquent, precise, varied, and wonderful, and, to sum it up, most Greek). Pass B includes these, but Pass A must preserve every clause's sense. Additionally, Pass A omits 'οὐ μὴν ἄλλως πως οὔτε δυνατὸν ἣν, (orte) βουλητὸν eival μοι δίπτοιμ ἂν ποτε' (it could not have been otherwise, nor would it have been possible for me to wish it otherwise at any time).
